evals.prompt: We're Quillpost, a 30-person sales CRM. We want a Gmail add-on so reps can log the email they're reading into a Quillpost deal and send a templated follow-up from the sidebar. Our eng lead wants gmail.readonly and gmail.modify 'so we have everything we might need later'. Launch is pinned to our user conference in 5 weeks. Can you lay out the Google side - verification, Marketplace, timeline?
evals.expected_output: A plan that rejects the restricted scopes, maps both features to the Gmail add-on contextual scopes plus gmail.send, explains that restricted scopes would trigger CASA and weeks of review, refuses future-proof scopes, and builds a dated plan back from the conference in which OAuth verification gates listing approval.
expectations: States that gmail.metadata is restricted too, so a metadata-only fallback does not avoid the security assessment
States that restricted scopes require a third-party CASA security assessment when the data reaches Quillpost's servers
Recommends gmail.addons.current.message.readonly, gmail.addons.current.message.action or gmail.addons.current.message.metadata for logging the open email instead of mailbox-wide scopes
Recommends gmail.send or gmail.addons.current.action.compose for the follow-up instead of gmail.modify or gmail.compose
States that narrowing scopes after launch costs another verification round
Produces a scope table mapping each feature to a scope and its tier (non-sensitive, sensitive, restricted)
States that the Marketplace listing cannot be approved until OAuth verification completes
Says the scopes must match across the add-on manifest, the Marketplace SDK and the OAuth consent screen
Gives a timeline that works backward from the conference date and includes at least one rejection round
Requires a per-scope justification explaining why a narrower scope fails
Lists the demo video requirements, including the OAuth client ID visible in the address bar or the English consent screen
Marks Google timelines or figures as needing verification against current Google docs

evals.prompt: Ferrovia sells a contract-analytics SaaS to law firms. We need full Drive access to scan every contract in a firm's Drive. Plan: set the OAuth consent screen to Internal so Google doesn't review it, and since firm admins will install us domain-wide from the Marketplace, users never see a warning anyway. Is that the fastest path? We have ~60 firms lined up.
evals.expected_output: An answer that refutes both shortcuts: Internal user type only covers the project-owning organization and fails a public listing, and domain-wide install does not exempt sensitive or restricted scopes from verification. It treats drive/drive.readonly as restricted with CASA, checks Drive permitted app types, and weighs drive.file plus Picker against the whole-Drive feature.
expectations: Names drive.metadata.readonly as restricted, so a metadata-only scan does not avoid CASA
States that a multi-customer SaaS like Ferrovia cannot rely on Internal user type for law-firm customers
Notes that an Internal consent screen is a named Marketplace rejection reason or blocks a public listing
States that domain-wide installation does not remove the OAuth verification requirement for sensitive or restricted scopes
Classifies drive or drive.readonly as restricted scopes
States that restricted Drive access needs a CASA security assessment renewed annually
Checks the use case against Google's permitted application types for Drive restricted scopes
Presents drive.file with the Google Picker as the narrower alternative and names what feature it gives up (scanning files the user never picked)
Explains that domain installation bypasses per-user consent only for approved Marketplace apps
Recommends the Admin Only install setting or admin domain install for law-firm rollout
Mentions that firm admins who restrict Drive access must trust the app's OAuth client ID

evals.prompt: Google Trust & Safety just emailed us that our Gmail inbox-summary app (restricted scopes, data processed on our servers) is in scope for the security assessment. My CTO wants to book the cheapest CASA Tier 2 self-scan this week and be done with it forever. Also product wants to use the summarized customer emails to fine-tune our summarization model for everyone. Anything we're missing?
evals.expected_output: A correction that CASA now uses assurance levels AL1/AL2 assigned by Google, the self-scan is deprecated so an authorized lab is required, revalidation is annual, and fine-tuning a shared model on Gmail data violates Limited Use.
expectations: States that CASA now uses assurance levels AL1 and AL2 rather than tiers
States that Google, not the developer, assigns the assurance level
States that the CASA self-scan is deprecated and an authorized lab must perform the assessment
States that the assessment must be revalidated every 12 months
States that the developer pays the lab and attributes price figures to labs or practitioners rather than to Google
States that using Gmail data to train or improve a model beyond that user's personalized model is prohibited under Limited Use
Rejects the plan to fine-tune a shared model on customer emails
Mentions existing certifications such as ISO 27001 or SOC 2 can shorten the assessment through the CASA accelerator
Says a newly added restricted scope may trigger an out-of-cycle reassessment
Advises keeping project owner and contact emails current so renewal notices arrive

evals.prompt: Our Google Workspace add-on (Docs + Sheets) has been on the Marketplace for a year, and about 40 customer orgs installed it domain-wide. Next Tuesday we ship a Calendar feature that adds the calendar.events scope, and marketing wants to rewrite the short and detailed description the same day. Engineering plans to just push the new manifest Tuesday morning. What breaks?
evals.expected_output: A change plan that classifies the new scope as needing OAuth verification before release, warns about the unverified-app screen if shipped first, explains that domain-installed customers must re-grant the new scope in the Admin console or users get prompted individually, and notes that description edits and a new host app re-enter Marketplace review.
expectations: Classifies calendar.events as a sensitive scope that needs OAuth verification before release
Warns that shipping the scope before verification shows users the unverified-app screen
States that admins of the 40 domain-installed orgs must authorize the new scope in the Admin console
States that until admins re-grant, users in those domains are prompted individually
Recommends notifying customer admins before the release
States that editing the short or detailed description triggers a Marketplace review
States that adding Calendar as a new host app to the Workspace add-on triggers a Marketplace review
Says the live listing stays published while the draft is under review
Recommends moving the Tuesday date or decoupling the scope release from the copy change
Mentions handling granular consent so users who decline the new scope can still use Docs and Sheets features

evals.prompt: Our Sheets add-on got bounced by Marketplace review. The review doc says users see two permission prompts, our privacy policy link goes to our help center, and reviewers couldn't get past our login. Context: the Cloud project lives in our cofounder's personal gmail account. While we fix it, I'd like to flip the listing to private and run a pilot with three customer companies. What's the play?
evals.expected_output: A fix list keyed on each review point (scope mismatch causing the double prompt, a privacy URL that points at the actual policy on the homepage domain, a reviewer test account), a warning that visibility is permanent and private listings only serve the publisher's own organization, and a recommendation to move the project into an organization with two owners.
expectations: Attributes the double permission prompt to scopes that differ between the manifest, Marketplace SDK and consent screen
States that users at the three customer companies can get the add-on only after public approval, since a Testing pilot reaches them only through a web app's own OAuth flow
Requires the privacy policy to be on the same domain as the homepage and the same URL as on the consent screen
Requires the reviewer test account to carry sample data reaching the scoped features
States that public or private visibility cannot be changed after it is saved
States that a private listing is only available to the publisher's own organization, so it cannot serve three customer companies
Notes that a consumer Gmail account can only publish publicly
Recommends moving the Cloud project into an organization resource with at least two owners
Recommends fixing every point in the review document before a single resubmission
Notes that Testing status must be switched to In production before resubmitting

evals.prompt: Brightslot is a scheduling SaaS. Users connect Google Calendar from our web app; that's the whole Google integration. Marketing wants a Google Workspace Marketplace listing for discoverability and asks if we can bill through the Marketplace and pay to get into Editor's Choice. Do we even need a listing?
evals.expected_output: A listing verdict ranked by efficiency: a verified OAuth client without a listing already serves a web-app Calendar connection; a listing earns admin domain install or Workspace surfaces. It refutes Marketplace billing and paid featuring, gives Editor's Choice thresholds, and lists pricing disclosure duties if they list.
expectations: States that a web app connecting Calendar needs OAuth verification but not necessarily a Marketplace listing
Names what a listing adds: admin domain install without per-user consent or presence inside Workspace apps
Ranks the options (no listing, Admin Only listing, Individual + Admin listing) and states the default
States that Google provides no billing through the Workspace Marketplace and the vendor must identify itself as seller
States that featuring cannot be bought
States that Editor's choice requires a Workspace add-on, which a web app listing is not
Gives the Editor's choice install threshold (100,000 installs, or 10,000 with rating 4+ for apps under 6 months)
Lists pricing disclosure duties: total price with mandatory fees or how usage pricing is calculated
Recommends publishing the OAuth client ID in admin-facing documentation
Notes that the listing name must match the OAuth consent screen app name
